doc.title: Chuck Mancuso interviewed by Monk Rowe, Buffalo, New York, October 10, 2013

title: Seeing the Three Sounds at the Bonton in Buffalo
summary: Memorable club night hearing Gene Harris and the Three Sounds on East Ferry, plus bringing touring musicians to the gym at the Royal Arms.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Tell me about some of your most memorable moments in the jazz clubs in Buffalo. I mean is there some night, some artist that stands out in your head?

Oh my God. First time I went to the Bonton on Waverly Street on the east side, it was just like a typical New York or New Jersey bar on a corner. You walk in, there’s a long bar, there’s a back room where you might have a fish fry, etcetera. Well they had put up a little stage this high, so they could get some outlets in. And this seems to be — there was no ad for it, I somehow found out the Three Sounds — Gene Harris and Simpkins and Dowdy were playing. And I was taking piano lessons at the time. And Tom Jones, he was the sixth man. He could always get in free, and I’d give him these blind passes. And he was taking piano lessons. One of us loved Les McCann and one of us loved Gene Harris and we’d talk, who was the funkiest of them. So we’d have these fights. So I said, “Well let’s go see my man Gene, because he’s playing with the Three Sounds at this place and we’ll find it, we know where the hell it is, it’s on East Ferry. How hard can it be? They had the piano, they didn’t even have that set up yet. That’s how, this piano, was right on the floor. And they came out, three of them. And I looked around, it’s 9:30, there’s only like five people in the joint. I was to find out that the black audience comes out a little bit later. 9:30. So we’re right next to them, and it was an old piano, and he was hitting the keys so hard that a couple of the — you know it was not a good piano and these keys were like flying, ivory was flying — not a hundred of them but you know, five or six of them. I go, he’s beating the piano fucking up, Tom, look at that. I know Les is good, but look at this. And they just, I mean I was just blown away. And if he was here, we were here, I love him. Holy smokes. And then I met him and I interviewed him a little bit. And when he came in to the Royal Arms, which was a bigger club off of Main Street on West Utica, I think he wanted to work out and we had a trainer named Tony Sartori who also loved jazz. And I called up Tony and I says, Tony, these guys, a lot of them come in from out of town and I ask them if they’re athletes or anything and they didn’t have health clubs in those days, you know you had to go to the YMCA if you weren’t a member. So he said, “Charlie, you know I like the Three Sounds, bring him down, I’ll get him in the gym and we’ll do some stuff.” And Johnny Lytle was like that too he had been in Pittsburgh, sort of a boxer or something like that.
